newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economy grows, unemployment still high.
newsitem.headline: German economy grows, unemployment still high.

text.p: The German economy rebounded more strongly than expected in the second quarter of the year, official data showed on Thursday, but continued high unemployment in August left little reason for cheer.

Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 1.5 percent from the first quarter and 1.2 percent from the same quarter a year ago, after shrinking 0.5 percent in the first quarter from the quarter before and only growing 0.2 percent year-on-year.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said full-year growth for 1996 could well be stronger than the government's previous forecast of 0.75 percent.
The good news of the rebound was partly overshadowed by the more recent unemployment data, which showed continued weakness.

The number of jobless rose 14,000 to 3.939 million last month on a seasonally adjusted basis, the Federal Labour Office said. The adjusted unemployment rate was unchanged at 10.3 percent of the workforce.
Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said September data should show a seasonal improvement over August but the economic upturn was unlikely to have an immediate impact on unemployment.
"Unemployment figures tend to be a late indicator and we know it won't be just a couple of weeks (before we see an impact)," Jagoda told a news conference.
Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said the fight against unemployment remained Chancellor Helmut Kohl's most important domestic goal.
"But this will not be achieved without austerity measures," Hausmann said. "The Programme for More Jobs and Growth will be steadily implemented."
Unions plan mass protests in several major cities this weekend against the government's unpopular savings measures, which they say will boost, not reduce, joblessness.
The German data painted a sharp contrast to neighbouring France, where GDP shrank 0.4 percent in the first quarter from the previous quarter as record unemployment sapped consumer confidence.
Both countries have their work cut out if they are to qualify for European monetary union, which has no hope of succeeding without them.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, in an annual report on the German economy, said Germany could just meet the EMU criteria if it implements all its planned austerity measures.
The OECD report forecast 0.5 percent German growth for 1996, but officials said that figure could be revised upward in view of the strong second-quarter data.
